articles.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
articles.summary: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.
articles.body:
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.

Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.

Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.

Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.

Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory

What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong

Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.

On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.

He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.

A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.

Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.

Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.

Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.

These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.

Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.

On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability".

Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling.

Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, says she is "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict.

"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC.

Human Rights Watch described the ruling as "cruel and unjust".

"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.

The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years , also for colluding with foreign forces.

Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.

However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.

In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.

The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.

By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.

In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.

But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".

"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.

Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.

Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.

Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.

On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.

Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.

Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.

On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.

"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."

articles.title: 'Shawarma law' not 'Sharia law': Abdul El-Sayed's remark goes viral after senate win - watch

articles.body: The US midterm elections have delivered a major victory for Democrats, with the party making significant gains across the country and flipping control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.Among the notable victories was that of Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, whose remarks about implementing "shawarma law" instead of "Sharia law" have gone viral on social media.El-Sayed, 42, an epidemiologist and former public health official aligned with the Democratic Party's progressive wing, defeated Republican candidate and former representative Mike Rogers in one of the country's closely watched Senate races, NBC News projected. His victory makes him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.In his victory speech, El-Sayed introduced himself by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, before using Arabic expressions to take a swipe at Republicans and Vice-President JD Vance.“My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed,” he said, before explaining his repeated use of the Arabic expression "inshallah", meaning "God willing", during the campaign.“Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say “inshallah”, or “God willing”, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into alhamdulillah. For the rightwing ops, that just means “praise be to God,” OK?”He continued his remarks with a reference to Vance, saying, “JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.”El-Sayed also used his speech to criticise US support for Israel and speak about the situation in Gaza, condemning the abuse faced by those who have raised concerns about the conflict.“See, they try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” he said.“Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here, and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”El-Sayed's victory came despite a campaign marked by Islamophobic attacks from President Donald Trump and other Republicans. Trump had called him a “communist” and described him as a “jihadist” and a member of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood.He also faced a setback in the final days of the campaign when Democratic Representative Haley Stevens, whom he had defeated in the party's primary, withdrew her support and endorsed Rogers after attending church with the Republican candidate.El-Sayed had defeated Stevens to secure the Democratic nomination earlier this year, challenging the party establishment with a campaign centred on progressive policies. He advocated for universal healthcare through the Medicare for All proposal and called for an end to US military aid to Israel.Republicans had portrayed the general election as a referendum on the Democratic Party's progressive wing, making the contest between El-Sayed and Rogers one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.His win also extends the Republican Party's long-running electoral drought in Michigan. Republicans have not won a Senate seat in the state since 1994. El-Sayed will succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.His victory was among several electoral breakthroughs for women, candidates of colour and other underrepresented groups in Tuesday's elections. Democrats made significant gains in key statewide races and flipped control of both chambers of Congress, riding a wave of dissatisfaction with the Trump administration.The results also pointed to gains for Democrats in traditionally conservative states, with analysts, civil rights leaders and grassroots voter organisations suggesting that the party had attracted Republican voters while rebuilding support among its traditional constituencies.Black and Latino voters, in particular, had emerged as increasingly contested groups in recent election cycles, as the latest results reshaped the political landscape and expanded representation in the highest levels of American government.You use AI every day. articles.title: A millionaire businessman installed an electric fence around his £44.5 million Notting Hill mansion to keep foxes away; neighbours say it looks like a prisoner-of-war camp
articles.summary: A millionaire businessman has put up an electric fence around his £44 million mansion in Notting Hill, west London, to keep foxes away.
articles.body: A millionaire businessman has put up an electric fence around his £44 million mansion in Notting Hill, west London, to keep foxes away. David Walsh, who bought the four-storey property with his wife, Jyotsna Chadha, in 2023, gave “fox prevention purposes” as the reason in planning documents. Neighbours have called the fence ugly and likened it to a prisoner-of-war camp, while Kensington and Chelsea Council described it as an unwelcome addition. According to The Sun, Mr Walsh says the council looked at the wrong photographs. The Ladbroke Association has also raised public safety concerns about the barrier.Why did neighbours hate the millionaire’s electric fenceNeighbours in the area have called the fence ugly and likened its appearance to that of a prisoner-of-war camp. According to the report, the local authority, Kensington and Chelsea Council, described the installation as an unwelcome addition to the area.The report states that the council's enforcement papers suggested the fence would amount to a fortification of the property. The council said its design, height and prominent position would fail to preserve the character and appearance of the building, the street scene and the wider conservation area.Why did Mr Walsh defend installing the electric fenceMr Walsh told the Daily Mail that his wife is very frightened of foxes and that the matter was none of the council's business. He also said the council had become confused and had looked at the wrong photographs in the planning application.The report quotes Mr Walsh as saying he has a much better and more discreet plan, which he claims the council overlooked because of those photographs. According to The Sun, the fence is reportedly supported by his immediate neighbour, whose boundary wall is being used for the equipment. The report adds that Mr Walsh agreed with the measure and said he was tired of foxes digging through the rubbish.Why did the Ladbroke Association oppose the electric fenceThe Ladbroke Association, a community group founded in 1969 to care for the beauty, history and character of the neighbourhood, objected to the fence. According to the report, the group raised public safety concerns and the potential danger to people walking past the home.The association called for conditions requiring a minimum strength of current and adequate public liability insurance. It said it was surprised that the officers' report treated this as outside the scope of the planning assessment. According to The Sun, the group believes public safety should be a material planning consideration in this case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2024, cyber fraudsters siphoned Rs 5.44 lakh from a woman’s Canara Bank account; two years later, consumer commission orders bank to refund, pay Rs 1 lakh compensation and Rs 50,000 legal costs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Delhi has directed Canara Bank to refund Rs 4.14 lakh to a woman who lost Rs 5.44 lakh in two unauthorised
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Delhi has directed Canara Bank to refund Rs 4.14 lakh to a woman who lost Rs 5.44 lakh in two unauthorised transactions after receiving a fraudulent call. It held that the bank could not shift the entire loss onto her merely because the transactions were authenticated using her banking credentials, as it failed to produce complete technical records establishing her voluntary authorisation or negligence.Case backgroundAs per the commission order, Vinita, a savings account holder with Canara Bank, received a fraudulent call on April 7, 2024, around 4 pm. The following morning, two unauthorised transactions of Rs 5 lakh and Rs 44,488 were made from her account through IMPS.She immediately reported the fraud to the Cyber Crime Helpline and approached the bank, requesting that her account be blocked. However, she alleged that the officials at the nearest branch failed to provide timely assistance and directed her to the Ganga Ram Hospital branch.By the time the account was blocked, Rs 5.44 lakh had been debited. Despite repeated follow-ups, only Rs 1.30 lakh, which had been placed on hold, was recovered and credited to her account. The remaining Rs 4,14,488 was not refunded.Vinita approached the commission, alleging deficiency in banking services and seeking a refund of the unrecovered amount with interest, compensation for mental agony and litigation expenses.In its written statement, the bank argued that she had interacted with the fraudsters and shared her mobile screen with them, compromising her confidential banking credentials. It said the disputed transactions were authenticated using her MPIN/UPIN and OTPs and that it had blocked her account immediately after receiving her complaint.The bank relied on the RBI's July 6, 2017, circular on customer liability for unauthorised electronic banking transactions, arguing that losses arising from customer negligence had to be borne by the account holder until the fraud was reported.Commission's findingsThe bench comprising president Poonam Chaudhry and member Bariq Ahmad held that the bank had failed to establish that Vinita had voluntarily authorised the disputed transactions. It said authentication through banking credentials did not, by itself, prove that the account holder had consented to the transfers."Therefore, authentication and authorization cannot, in every case, be treated as synonymous," the bench observed.Relying on the national consumer commission's ruling in State Bank of India v. Pradosh Kumar Banerjee, the commission said technical authentication could not be equated with voluntary authorisation in cases involving deceptive cyber fraud.It noted that the bank had failed to produce IP logs, device verification records, beneficiary-addition logs, transaction audit trails and evidence showing whether the applicable cooling-off and fraud-monitoring safeguards had been followed.The bench also said that although sharing her mobile screen could amount to negligence under the RBI framework, the bank could not simply rely on credential authentication without establishing the precise circumstances in which the transactions were initiated."The complainant, on the other hand, reported the transactions promptly and approached the bank on the same date. The bank's reliance solely upon credential authentication, without producing the complete transaction audit trail and relevant security records, is insufficient to discharge its evidentiary burden in the facts of the present case," the bench added.The commission rejected the bank's argument that the pending cybercrime investigation prevented it from deciding the consumer complaint. It said criminal proceedings against the fraudsters and proceedings concerning deficiency in banking services operated in different fields.It held that the bank had failed to establish that the entire loss resulted solely from the woman's negligence and that its failure to satisfactorily address the unauthorised transactions amounted to deficiency in service.Final orderAnnounced on October 28, 2026, the order allowed the complaint. The commission directed Canara Bank to pay:Rs 4,14,488, the unrecovered amount, with 9 percent annual interest from April 8, 2024, until realisation.Rs 1 lakh as compensation for mental agony, harassment and inconvenience.Rs 50,000 as litigation expenses.The bank must make the payment within 45 days, failing which the amount payable will carry further interest at 12 percent per annum from the date of default until realisation.

articles.title: Meta under scanner as Delhi Police files FIR over child abuse content: NHRC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Wednesday registered an FIR against Meta India over the availability of child sexual abuse material on its platforms, National
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Wednesday registered an FIR against Meta India over the availability of child sexual abuse material on its platforms, National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) member Priyank Kanoongo informed.“Acting on our directions, Delhi Police has registered an FIR regarding the availability of Child Sexual Exploitative and Abuse Material (CSEAM) on platforms operated by Meta India,” Kanoongo said in a post on X.The development comes amid growing scrutiny of social media platforms over the circulation of child sexual abuse material and the use of online advertisements to direct users to illegal content.Earlier, on September 16, the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) had summoned the Managing Director and Head of Meta India in connection with its inquiry.Between January and June 2026, Meta took action against 5.3 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content on Facebook and Instagram in India.Meta has said online predators are increasingly using advertisements to evade detection, disguising them as harmless content while directing users to illegal material hosted on external websites.It has also committed to reporting child safety cases directly to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, operated by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C).Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Between 1984 and 1989, Oregon recycled the old asphalt on about 672 km (420 miles) of country roads, and over 75 percent of those projects were later rated fair or better
articles.summary: Discover how Oregon successfully recycled old asphalt on country roads between 1984 and 1989, achieving over 75% success rating. Learn about the cold in-place recycling method and its benefits for low-volume roads.
articles.body: Few things test a driver's patience like a cracked, bumpy country road. In the 1980s, Oregon found a way to give these roads a second job. The Federal Highway Administration’s guide, ‘User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction,’ says that between 1984 and 1989 the state recycled the old asphalt on about 672 km (420 miles) of low-volume roads, the kind people call country roads. More than 75 percent of those projects were later graded fair or better. That's not a perfect score. Still, it shows how recycling worn pavement can be a good, workable option for roads with lighter traffic.How the recycling actually works The method is called cold in-place recycling. It may sound complicated, but it’s actually pretty simple. Instead of removing old pavement, the worn-out top layer is ground up on site. The federal guide states that this fix is used when the depth of the damage is about 4 to 6 inches (100 to 150 mm). The crushed asphalt is mixed with new asphalt in either liquid or foamed state without any heating. Then the mixture is placed back in place and compacted with heavy rollers. The work is done on-site, so there are no long truck trips to a far-away plant. After a couple of weeks of curing in favourable conditions, according to the federal guide, a hot mix overlay is added on top. In most cases in Oregon, however, as stated in a 1991 article, the recycling layer was sealed with a sand or chip seal coating.Why quiet country roads were a good match Oregon kept this work on lightly travelled roads. In their 1991 Transportation Research Record paper, authors Todd Scholz, R. Gary Hicks, David Rogge and Dale Allen explained that every Oregon project was partial depth recycling. These roads generally carried fewer than 2,000 vehicles per day. Projects were also completed on county roads and US Forest Service roads. The authors also reported construction costs of approximately $1.70 to $2.10 per square yard. A normal 2-inch asphalt overlay was about $2.75 to $4.00 per square yard. These figures reflect prices at the time. The method has been studied closely by the Oregon State Highway Division and Oregon State University since 1986. The authors concluded that it seemed to be a viable option for low-volume roads. The federal guide also said that taking old asphalt to a plant on small roads will likely cost more. This makes fixing the road in place all the more tempting.What the ratings do and do not tell us The fair or better rating is useful, but it does not always guarantee perfect roads. The federal guide was careful about this point. It says that the cold recycled mixes were not recommended for use as a wearing course, which means that it must be protected by an overlay. Choosing the right road is also quite important. A road with a failing base or subgrade cannot be fixed by simply recycling the surface. The guide noted that eight projects in Pennsylvania received good to satisfactory ratings if a double seal coat was applied over the recycled mix. It also explained that more performance information was needed on resistance to rutting, fatigue and durability. The administration guide further added that more study was also needed on how cold recycled mixes would perform on busier roads. Oregon’s story is not about some magic fix. It's about a practical tool that, when crews chose the right roads, got fair or better ratings on most projects. That's good news to anyone who has dodged potholes on a back road.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: POST SCRIPT | A suitable hire, a not-so suitable employer
articles.summary: Anyone who has tried hiring Gen Z in India lately will have noticed that the correspondence has developed a genre of its own, and that the genre is not,
articles.body: Anyone who has tried hiring Gen Z in India lately will have noticed that the correspondence has developed a genre of its own, and that the genre is not, as one had innocently assumed, the job application. It is the reply to a Sunday matrimonial advertisement, written by someone who isn’t entirely sure they wish to get married, has not read the particulars of the prospective spouse, and would like to know whether the arrangement can be conducted remotely.I don’t offer this as a flourish. Indian hiring has always been an arranged marriage on better stationery, and in a country where a 2018 survey of more than 160,000 households found 93% of married couples describing their marriages as arranged, the template needs little explaining.The job description is the Sunday matrimonial ad, with “fair, homely, convent-educated” replaced by “dynamic, self-starting, comfortable with ambiguity”, the last of which means nobody at the company has decided what the job is, though everyone is agreed that somebody should do it. The placement consultant is the ghatak, the Bengali matchmaker, who has met neither party properly, knows next to nothing about either, and is prepared to stake his reputation, such as it is, on their compatibility. He will subsequently collect his fee and disappear, leaving two families to discover that the boy drinks.The interview panel is konye dekha, at which a girl was once asked to walk across the room and sing a line of Rabindrasangeet, presumably to establish that her legs and vocal cords were in working order. The contemporary candidate is asked for a free three-day assignment, the principal difference being that no prospective father-in-law ever recorded the song and incorporated it into a client presentation. The notice-period buyout is the last bride price still paid in polite company, and the annual appraisal is the occasion on which the in-laws explain why one has not quite lived up to expectations.The latest specimens come courtesy of Amit Ray, whom I have theoretically known forever, our fathers having shared a school classroom. In Bengali society, this establishes a degree of intimacy that actual acquaintance frequently fails to achieve. It also constitutes an excellent reference check. A proposal accompanied by the information that the fathers went to school together would get past the first round in most respectable Bengali households, even if the prospective groom were currently wanted by the police.Practically, I follow Amit with considerable interest on LinkedIn, where he has just shared some questions from shortlisted applicants to his latest job post. He doesn’t specify their ages, and he hardly needs to. The correspondence has the unmistakable air of a generation that has arrived at the marriage market without first consulting its parents, the advertisement or, quite possibly, itself.One applicant writes: “I have a full time role. Is there any way to work around that?”This is rather like answering a matrimonial advertisement to enquire whether one’s existing spouse is likely to present an administrative difficulty. Amit’s response, “Yes, it’s called resigning”, is admirably economical and holds equally well in both institutions. There is little to improve upon it, except perhaps to add that the first spouse should ideally be informed.Corporate India, incidentally, arrived at this metaphor before I did. When the moonlighting controversy broke in 2022, Infosys told its staff “No two-timing”, while Wipro chairman Rishad Premji called the practice “cheating” and said 300 employees found working for a rival had been let go. One almost expected a joint statement from the aggrieved families, followed by a demand for the return of jewellery.Another applicant asks, “What is the role about?”The answer, unfortunately, sits directly below the headline in approximately 1,200 words, a length no Bengali matrimonial biodata has attempted even after including the grandfather’s service record, the maternal uncle’s posting in London and the family’s ancestral connection to a zamindari that ceased to exist before Independence.It is possible, of course, that the question is sincere. By last year, LinkedIn was receiving some 11,000 applications a minute, up 45% in twelve months, while some job seekers now employ AI agents to identify openings and apply on their behalf. We have reached the interesting stage of technological civilisation at which machines propose employment arrangements between people who may subsequently be required to meet one another.The applicant may therefore be hearing about the opportunity for the first time, rather like a Bengali son arriving home to discover that an aunt in Salt Lake has circulated his horoscope across three districts, shortlisted two suitable girls and enquired about the availability of a marriage hall. His participation, while desirable, is no longer essential to the proceedings.A third says, “I applied for the role but I don’t know if I’m a fit”, a doubt that earlier generations carried to the mandap and then kept to themselves for forty years.Of all the replies, this one may be the most honest sentence to pass through an Indian hiring process since liberalisation. Everybody else, after all, has been passionate about the company’s mission since birth, inspired by its leadership since nursery school and deeply committed to its values without having the faintest idea what it sells. This candidate has at least declined to manufacture an emotion for the benefit of Human Resources. Amit is nevertheless right that such candour, offered before the interview, does little to inspire confidence. Honesty is greatly admired in the Indian workplace, provided it is exercised somewhere else.A fourth applicant would like to meet the team, which is to say the in-laws, before proceeding further. There was a time when such a request would have caused considerable distress among the elders. The girl had been shown the boy’s photograph; his salary had been mentioned; the family priest had been consulted. What possible purpose could be served by meeting the people with whom she would be expected to spend the rest of her life?Then there is the ghosting, which Amit lists as his evergreen item: the old runaway groom, whose escape once demanded a night train, a false name and some nerve, and now requires nothing more strenuous than leaving a message on two blue ticks. Technology has done for cowardice what air-conditioning did for the Indian summer. It has made the activity considerably more comfortable.Before those of us past thirty climb too far up the high horse, however, I should declare an interest.I have spent 25 years in Indian media, which is longer than some of these applicants have been alive, and I regret to report that nobody under thirty invented any of this. We did. We invented the job description, that remarkable work of speculative fiction in which a self-starter with eight years’ experience, fifteen skills and the judgment of a seasoned professional is sought at a fresher’s salary. We invented the insistence that the candidate must be a team player, which frequently means agreeing with the captain even when he has steered the ship into a shopping mall.We invented “we are a family here”, which, upon closer examination, turns out to be literally true. Long hours, no boundaries, unsolicited advice, emotional blackmail and a scene if you try to leave. A particularly close-knit corporate family will even object to your having friends outside it. The only significant difference is that your actual family will generally feed you before beginning the interrogation.And we have been ghosting candidates for thirty years under the respectable corporate expression “we’ll get back to you”, which is the employment equivalent of the groom’s family saying they must consult an elderly aunt before committing. The aunt, naturally, is never heard from again.One recruitment trade report puts the proportion of Indian job seekers ghosted by employers at 73%. The great moral gulf between the generations, meanwhile, on figures reported by Newsweek, amounts to 41% of Gen Z job seekers admitting to having cut off a prospective employer, against 37% of millennials.Four percentage points. For this, apparently, civilisation is collapsing.That horse the millennials are now attempting to mount stands approximately four points high, and the difficulty of getting onto it may explain some of the shouting.Consider the boy’s side in its full glory.Infosys sent campus offer letters, some dated as early as April 2022, to more than 2,000 engineering graduates who, according to the employees’ union NITES, were still waiting to join more than two years later. In the intervening period, they were allegedly summoned for unpaid training and repeat assessments, rather as a prospective bride might be asked to demonstrate her cooking while the groom’s family continued to consider its options.Asked about the delay in August 2024, the chief executive offered the immortal explanation: “We changed some dates.”This is precisely what the groom’s father says when the wedding has been postponed for the third time, the caterer has been paid and the girl’s family has begun to suspect that something is amiss. Dates, in the Indian arranged marriage, are among the few things that can be changed without anyone accepting responsibility.In February 2025, more than 300 freshers were let go after failing an internal assessment in three attempts. Infosys maintained that the rule was in the contract and had existed for over two decades. NITES said the affected recruits belonged to the same delayed batch, having finally been onboarded in October 2024 after waiting more than two years.If the union’s account is correct, they had waited for over two years to be married and were returned to their parents within four months for failing an examination. A traditional Bengali household would at least have had the decency to blame the horoscope. It might also have returned the sweets.As for fidelity, the corporate India that sacks you for keeping a second employer is the same one in which, in a video that went viral in January 2025, L&T’s chairman regretted being unable to make staff work on Sundays and asked, “How long can you stare at your wife?”This was an extraordinary question from a man who appeared to be proposing that the employee spend considerably more time staring at him.Two-timing, it seems, is a sin only when the other party pays. The employer, meanwhile, would prefer that you abandon your spouse, neglect your children and regard Sunday as an unfortunate clerical error in the calendar. The employee must be monogamous; the company reserves the right to be possessive.L&T defended the remarks as being about nation-building, which is more or less how Indian marriages have always been explained. The individual may be miserable, but the institution must endure.And that, I think, is where the generational quarrel becomes interesting.We are offering an arranged marriage: total exclusivity, the joint family, a ninety-day notice period and the unilateral right to send you home. We would like unconditional commitment, preferably before disclosing the compensation, and we reserve the right to restructure the relationship whenever market conditions demand it. The bride must be flexible, the groom’s family is under considerable pressure, and the uncle who made all the promises has moved to another organisation.They have come looking for a situationship: no labels, options open, commitment negotiable, last seen yesterday. They would prefer to keep their evenings, meet the other members of the household and retain the right to discover, three weeks later, that they are no longer feeling it.Each side considers the other unserious, and each has assembled a perfectly respectable dossier in support of the accusation.Seen from their end, even the request to meet the team stops looking like impertinence and starts looking like elementary due diligence. In an arranged marriage, the trouble is seldom the boy in the biodata. He has a good job, a decent photograph and a smile that suggests somebody has just told him to smile. It is the household that does it. The mother who has opinions about breakfast. The father who expects gratitude for electricity. The aunt who visits for a fortnight and stays until somebody dies.Corporate culture is much the same. The offer letter describes the groom. The team is where you discover his family.None of this is absolution, and I do not propose to become one of those middle-aged gentlemen who mistake agreement with the young for evidence of their own youth. An applicant who cannot be bothered to read 1,200 words about their own future is unlikely to read the client’s brief either, and I would still prefer that whoever I hire turn up on the appointed day. Ideally sober, although twenty-five years in media have taught me to keep my expectations modest.With Amit’s inbox in front of me, I would be no kinder in the parentheses. I would ask the same questions, raise much the same objections and possibly say worse things afterwards to people I trusted. There are limits to my sympathy, and being an employer has not made me a saint. It has merely given me a better chair from which to practise hypocrisy.But I have stopped pretending the rot began with them. The young have clearly studied everything we ever did to them.It is only the JD they skipped.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: 'I’ve been shot in the stomach': Haryana man dies after 3 men shoot him at bike repair shop
articles.summary: REWARI: A man was shot dead in broad daylight in Gokalgarh village of Haryana’s Rewari district on Wednesday.
articles.body: REWARI: A man was shot dead in broad daylight in Gokalgarh village of Haryana’s Rewari district on Wednesday.The victim had gone to a motorcycle repair shop to get his bike fixed when three men allegedly arrived on a motorcycle and confronted him. One of them reportedly pulled out a firearm and shot him in the stomach.Despite being critically injured, the victim managed to call his mother and inform her that he had been shot. He subsequently called a friend and told him about the incident. He died during treatment at around 5 pm.The deceased was identified as Manoj, a resident of Gokalgarh village. Sadar police station registered a murder case on the complaint of his father, Jaswant Singh. In his complaint, the father named Manindra as the alleged shooter, while Vishal (21) and Mahesh (27) were also named as accomplices.According to information, Manoj had reached Garima Bike Repairing Centre in Gokalgarh village on Wednesday afternoon to get his motorcycle repaired. Several other people were also present at the shop when Manindra, Vishal and Mahesh, all residents of the village, allegedly arrived.The three reportedly surveyed the surroundings before Manindra allegedly pulled out a firearm and shot Manoj in the stomach. The trio then fled on a motorcycle within seconds.After being shot, Manoj first called his mother and told her that he had been shot in the stomach. He subsequently called his village friend Abhishek and informed him about the incident.Abhishek immediately rushed to the spot and took Manoj to Rewari Civil Hospital. Given his critical condition, doctors referred him to Virat Hospital. However, he succumbed to his injuries at around 5 pm during treatment.Rewari SP Hemendra Kumar said he immediately reached the spot and conducted a detailed inspection of the crime scene. An FIR for murder has been registered at Sadar police station on the basis of the complaint filed by Manoj’s father.A forensic team was called to the crime scene and collected samples and other evidence. The SP said four police teams had been constituted to apprehend the accused, with each team working in a different direction. Sadar police station SHO PSI Rakesh Kumar is also part of the investigation. Police are making efforts to arrest the accused at the earliest.Police are also scanning CCTV footage from cameras installed in and around the area to gather clues about the suspects and their escape route.The body has been kept at Rewari Civil Hospital, and a post-mortem examination is scheduled for Thursday. The investigation is underway.Manoj’s criminal background has also emerged during the investigation. He was reportedly associated with a gang, though the nature of his alleged association is yet to be established. He was arrested and sent to jail in October 2025 in connection with the murder of Bhura, a fellow villager. He secured bail and walked out of jail around one-and-a-half months ago.In his complaint, Jaswant Singh alleged that Manindra had shot his son, while Vishal and Mahesh had accompanied him. articles.title: Crowborough designer's 'thumb almost held up a Batman film'
articles.summary: Costume designer Vin Burnham tells the BBC how she accidentally damaged Batman's cowl.
articles.body:
Vin Burnham has made a name for herself as a costume designer behind some big Hollywood blockbusters and hits on both the stage and screen.

And her decades-long career has seen her collect a rich seam of stories, including the time she nearly accidentally delayed the filming of a Batman movie.

Burnham helped create the iconic Batsuit worn by Michael Keaton in Tim Burton's Batman, which she later refined for the sequel Batman Returns.

On the very first day of filming Batman, she said she was in the dressing room getting the cowl ready when she mistakenly put her thumb through the front of it.

"There was only one and that is a complete crime," Burnham added.

However, Keaton had forgotten his contact lenses, which gave her time to make the necessary repairs, she said.

Burnham, who lives near Crowborough in East Sussex, has also designed Aslan for the BBC's The Chronicles of Narnia, alongside costumes for the BBC's Wind in The Willows.

She said she was "very, very fond" of Aslan.

"To me he's a bit more golden retriever than a lion," Burnham continued.

Children used to write fan letters to him, she told BBC South East .

Burnham says on her website that after starting out in the props department at the Royal Opera House as a trainee, she has since "dyed, painted, stitched and glued [her] way up through the ranks".

Among her proudest achievements is designing Lady Gaga's "living dress" for the Monster Ball World Tour, besides her work for the BBC.

"Everything about a costume is as important as a word in a script," she said.

"The whole point of theatre and film is storytelling - and costume designers are storytellers," Burnham continued.

articles.title: Henry Nowak's killer's appeal 'ludicrous', says family
articles.summary: Vickrum Digwa, who was sentenced to life in prison for murdering Henry Nowak, appeals his sentence.
articles.body:
Henry Nowak's family say it is "ludicrous" their son's killer is being allowed to appeal against his sentence and it is a "disgrace" his mother, who hid the murder weapon, will be released from prison early.

Vickrum Digwa, 23, was found guilty of the 18-year-old student's murder and sentenced to life in prison , with a 21-year minimum term, earlier this year.

He is appealing against his sentence on Thursday, arguing that it is too severe.

Digwa stabbed Henry, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, five times with an eight-inch blade in Southampton on 3 December – and lied to police that the student had started the altercation and racially abused him.

In an interview with ITV News' UK Editor, Paul Brand, Henry's stepmother, Katie Nowak says: "It just doesn't feel fair to us at all.

"It's another process that we've got to go through. It's another fight that we have to have.

"It was a very clear verdict. It's not right that he's allowed to do this."

The court will also consider a referral by the Attorney General, who argues that Digwa's sentence was unduly lenient.

Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, was sentenced to three years in prison in July for assisting an offender, after she hid the blade Digwa used to kill Henry.

Henry's mother, Lucy Ross told ITV News, "Mother to mother – she is no mother."

"We all protect our children, but we also protect our children from right and wrong."

"But she never did the right thing. She hid the knife, which had Henry's blood on it."

ITV News last month revealed that Kaur will be freed this December , after serving just one year of her sentence, as part of the government's early release scheme.

It's a date that feels "particularly cruel" to the Nowaks, falling around the anniversary of Henry's murder.

Lucy Ross told Paul Brand: "As soon as she gets out, she could arrange a visiting order to go see [Digwa]."

"She's lucky enough that she could go and see her boy. I have to go to Henry's grave to see Henry."

Henry's father, Mark Nowak, echoed this: "It's an absolute disgrace. Let's be honest."

"She'll be out in December of this year having received a three-year sentence. How on earth can that be right?"

"She'll be out for Christmas, and I won't have Christmas with Henry."

Henry's family told ITV News the government needs to seriously rethink its decision to allow Kaur's early release - and the scheme as a whole.

Katie Nowak, Henry's stepmother, says, "I'd say that victims need to have far more weight and thought given to how they feel."

"Because throughout this whole process, it doesn't feel like anyone's on your side."

Under the Sentencing Act 2026, which came into force on 1 October, most prisoners serving fixed-term sentences of up to two and a half years are automatically released on licence after serving a third of the time, rather than half.

Kaur, who is appealing against her sentence, would serve the rest of it in the community on licence, and could be recalled to prison if she breached her licence conditions.

She spent 221 days on remand, which the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said was taken into account when she was sentenced.

Her crime of assisting an offender is not one of the offences excluded from changes to the early release scheme.

articles.title: Wildfire-hit Fylingdales Moor added to heritage risk register
articles.summary: Parts of Fylingdales Moor are added to Historic England's at-risk register after a major wildfire.
articles.body:
Parts of the North York Moors landscape have been added to Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register, after a wildfire caused extensive damage.

The blaze burned across about seven sq miles (18 sq km), of Fylingdales Moor in 2025, damaging peatland habitats, more than 20 scheduled monuments and six listed buildings.

Historic England and the North York Moors National Park Authority (NYMNPA), are using drone technology to assess the impact.

"The Heritage at Risk Register showcases the positive impact that restoring and reusing these special places can have," Historic England said.

A large area of Fylingdales Moor was added to the register following the wildfire which started in early August 2025 and burned for more than 40 days, spreading through parts of the North York Moors National Park.

An investigation later concluded it was likely to have been caused by someone using a campfire or gas burner.

The annual Heritage at Risk Register identifies buildings, monuments and landscapes considered vulnerable because of neglect, decay, damage or other threats.

It also highlights sites where progress is being made to secure their future.

Historic England is supporting the NYMNPA with drone-based Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) technology and aerial imagery to assess the extent of the damage.

It said the loss of vegetation and peat had exposed archaeological remains previously hidden beneath the moorland, and that surveys were helping specialists record and assess them while building a clearer picture of the fire's impact on the landscape.

Elsewhere on this year's register, Historic England said significant progress had been made towards securing the future of Wakefield's former Crown Court House, which could be removed from the list once restoration work was complete.

Built in 1810, the Grade II listed building on Wood Street is undergoing restoration more than 30 years after it closed. It served as Wakefield's local court and crown court until 1992.

Work is under way to convert the building into a venue known as the Court House, incorporating a bar, restaurant, workspace, community hall and creative studios.

articles.title: Has India’s democracy failed its Muslims? Jailed scholar triggers debate
articles.summary: Sharjeel Imam questioned foundational ideas of India’s nationalism in interview with The Quint, inspiring heated debate.
articles.body:
Has the world’s largest democracy failed the world’s largest minority – its nearly 200 million Muslims? That question is at the heart of a polarising debate currently under way in India.

The debate started with Sharjeel Imam, a 38-year-old Muslim scholar, who gave a lengthy interview to an Indian news website on September 29 from his prison cell in New Delhi.

Imam covered a wide range of issues and raised uncomfortable questions about the place of the country’s Muslim minority, which forms roughly 14 percent of India’s 1.4 billion population.

“There are around 210 million Muslims in India – one of the biggest Muslim groups in the world, with practically zero say in this democracy,” Imam told the Indian news outlet, The Quint .

He criticised the Indian constitution for its “enshrined centralisation” of power and called its brand of secularism “particularly Islamophobic and parochial”, adding that democracy was a tool to deny Muslims their political representation and rights.

Hailing from Jahanabad district of Bihar, India’s poorest state, Imam graduated from the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay in computer science and worked as a software engineer before returning to academics. As a doctoral student at the Centre for Historical Studies at New Delhi-based Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), his primary research area was the political history of India’s Muslims.

In 2019, months after winning a second term in office, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government passed a controversial citizenship law, which granted an expedited pathway to Indian citizenship for non-Muslim refugees from India’s neighbouring countries. The United Nations called the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) “fundamentally discriminatory” against Muslims.

The passage of the law ignited nationwide anti-CAA protests. Led by Muslims, mostly women, a weeks-long demonstration near Shaheen Bagh, a densely-populated Muslim ghetto on the southeastern edge of New Delhi, became the epicentre of those protests.

Imam was one of the chief organisers of the Shaheen Bagh sit-in. He was arrested in January 2020 for inciting violence through speeches made at the protests.

But there had been no violence until his arrest. It came the next month in northeast New Delhi where anti-CAA sit-ins organised in Muslim neighbourhoods were attacked by mobs, incited by hate speech from leaders from the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Despite him being already behind bars when the violence broke out, Imam was charged with rioting, murder, attempted murder, sedition, and “promoting enmity on grounds of religion” under several laws, including a stringent anti-terror law.

He was not the only one . Nearly a dozen Muslim students and activists, including another JNU scholar Umar Khalid , were arrested and imprisoned for being the alleged conspirators in the 2020 riots. They remain in jail without trial and repeatedly denied bail, with rights groups calling their continued incarceration a “gross abuse of power” and a glaring example of judicial oversight, in which the accused are “guilty until proven innocent”.

According to Imam, such an alleged abuse of power – especially targeting Muslims – is systemic and goes back to the very ideas behind the founding of India as a Hindu-majority country.

In his interview with The Quint, he called India’s independence icon Mahatma Gandhi a “fascist” for making Congress – the party that led India’s freedom struggle and currently in the opposition – an “essentially Hindu party” and for allegedly endorsing certain ideas and practices now pushed by Modi’s BJP and its ideological parent, the far-right Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).

Founded in 1925 along the lines of the fascist parties in Europe, the RSS aims to turn a constitutionally secular India into an ethnic Hindu state.

Imam also accused independent India’s first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru of “falsehood and mythmaking” for projecting India as an ancient, “uniquely tolerant” civilisation in his book, The Discovery of India.

But Imam reserved his most scathing attack for India’s pro-secular liberals, arguing that there is no difference between them and the supporters of the BJP and the RSS.

“In short, both secular and Hindutva frameworks share the same core ideas – the myth of uniformity, centralisation and denial of sharing of power,” he said. Hindutva refers to the Hindu supremacist movement championed by the RSS and the BJP in order to turn a constitutionally secular India into an ethnic Hindu state.

In a rebuttal in The Quint, legal scholar Mohd Zeeshan Ahmad said Imam “raises serious historical and ideological questions that cannot be evaded merely because he is facing prosecution,” but that his “equation of secularism with Hindutva is unpersuasive”.

“Imam’s language risks projecting Muslims as a homogeneous political bloc, obscuring disagreements of class, caste, gender, region and ideology,” Ahmad wrote.

“Where are the Pasmanda [less privileged castes] Muslims in this political imagination? Where is the question of gender justice, including the rights of women within Muslim communities? Who gets to speak for the ‘Qaum’ [community], and whose experiences are rendered invisible when a singular political voice claims to represent it?”

But Irfan Ahmad, professor of anthropology and sociology at Ibn Khaldun University in Istanbul, Turkiye, and author of several acclaimed books on the Muslim question in South Asia, told Al Jazeera that Imam is right in questioning whether there is a difference between the Congress and the BJP when it comes to secularism.

“Indian nationalism rests on a false division between ‘secular’ nationalism of the Congress, especially through its figures like Nehru and Gandhi, on the one hand, and ‘communal’ right-wing forces on the other,” he said.

“The fact is that from the beginning, the Congress had within what it depicted as its outside: ethno-racist-Hindu nationalists. The flow of leaders between the Congress and overtly Hindu parties was smooth,” he added, citing Lala Lajpat Rai, K M Munshi, Shyama Prasad Mookerjee, and Madan Mohan Malviya as examples.

“K B Hedgewar, the RSS founder, was himself earlier in the Congress.”

Ahmad, the professor, said the difference between the Congress and the BJP is “of the same nature as the one between Republicans and Democrats in the United States where both converge to advance ‘American interests’ and wage wars outside”.

“The problem Indian Muslims face is not of party politics but the very Indian/Hindu nationalism which all political parties, including the Left, subscribe to, albeit not identically,” he told Al Jazeera.

“If a democracy routinely makes a community, Muslims in this case, invisible in terms of representation in legislatures, then there is something fundamentally wrong with this democracy. Declining ratio of Muslims in parliament testifies to the silencing of Muslims.”

Ahmad says the “question worth asking is: how correct is the view of a secular India?”

On political empowerment of India’s Muslims

In his interview with The Quint, Imam suggested that India should have “constitutional republicanism” that guarantees decentralisation of power and more community rights. He argued that the 1947 partition of the Indian subcontinent – which gave birth to Muslim-majority Pakistan – “was forced by the Congress”.

He regarded Pakistan’s founding leader Muhammad Ali Jinnah as “a great, democratic leader” and poet-philosopher Muhammad Iqbal as his political inspiration. Calling for a faith-based separation of power, Imam underlined Iqbal’s call for the “creation of a Muslim India within India” and demanded proportional representation as opposed to the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system in Indian elections.

“As Iqbal and Jinnah rightly foresaw, FPTP with no safeguards will lead to permanent marginalisation of Muslims who were, even before partition, the hated minority, the hated ‘other’ of the emerging nationalist discourse,” he said. “History has proved them right.”

Responding to Imam, a columnist who goes by the pseudonym Ibn-e-Khaldun Bharati, wrote in The Print news website that Imam represents an “Islamist agenda” which “demands the status of a nation – a Pakistan within the borders of India”.

Calling him “unapologetically anti-liberal, anti-secular, anti-democracy, anti-constitution – in a word, anti-national,” Bharati claims Imam feels “an entitlement to the rulership of India, which has kept their thought-leaders confused about whether they are a nation or a minority”.

“A nation needs a state, whereas a minority needs constitutional guarantees. Neither in theory nor in practice can one be both at the same time,” he wrote. “But such has been the ingenuity of Muslim leaders that they have managed to be both simultaneously. They carved a country for themselves and also secured special privileges as a minority – a classic example of having one’s cake and eating it too.”

Questioning Bharati’s submission, political analyst Asim Ali pointed out “the Kafkaesque nature of the whole affair”.

“This is a man who has now been behind bars for six years ostensibly for a speech advocating a ‘chakka jam’ [road blockade] without any call for violence alongside the even more absurd charge of conspiring to incite the Delhi riots that took place a month after he was already in jail,” Ali wrote in a column for The Telegraph newspaper.

“The space of experience for Muslims like Imam includes not only their personal experiences of discrimination but also of what they have learned about the history of recurrent communal pogroms, the framing of Muslim men in terror cases, the brutalities by policemen and so on,” Ali wrote, citing several examples of police atrocities in the past decades.

While Ali argued that Imam’s depiction of Gandhi and Jinnah is “grossly distorted” and his reading of the pre-independence and partition history as “warped”, he conceded that there is “space for a person like Imam in a radical democratic project that strives for equality and liberty for everyone” in India.

“Imam envisages a role as the head of an intellectual pressure group of middle-class Muslim activists displacing the clerical establishment as the principal voice articulating a ‘positive’ agenda of ‘Muslim demands’,” Ali wrote.

Sharjeel Imam v Umar Khalid: The ‘model’ Muslim

When it comes to the question of future intellectual Muslim leadership, comparisons are often made between Imam and Khalid. Both of them are often accused of being the “masterminds” of the 2020 New Delhi riots and are currently in the same jail in the Indian capital.

But that is where their similarities end.

Khalid, 39, is a left-wing activist who does not reject the Indian constitution – or its version of democracy or secularism – as explicitly as Imam does. He has also frequently cited Gandhi and his message of non-violent resistance in his speeches and writings.

Khalid is hailed by India’s Marxists and liberals as a “model Muslim” who is being punished by an anti-Muslim government for his campaign against the BJP’s hate politics. Global figures and rights groups frequently call for Khalid’s release.

Among them is New York City’s mayor Zohran Mamdani, who, while delivering the inaugural keynote address at the Nelson Mandela Global Leadership Forum in July this year, questioned Khalid’s imprisonment.

“Why must we wait as Umar Khalid enters his sixth year of captivity in Delhi – a political prisoner jailed under the same manufactured charges of terrorism levelled against Madiba,” he said, using the name for Mandela commonly used by South Africans.

It was the second time Mamdani, who has Indian roots, had talked about Khalid since being elected as mayor. In January, he met his parents and left the following handwritten note for him: “Dear Umar, I think of your words on bitterness often, and the importance of not letting it consume one’s self. It was a pleasure to meet your parents. We are all thinking of you.”

Last month, Ireland-based human rights organisation Front Line Defenders in Dublin announced Khalid as the winner of the 2026 Award for Human Rights Defenders at Risk.

Imam does not evoke such global solidarities, which are mainly limited to India’s Muslim community.

“Take the example of Zohran Mamdani,” says Ahmad, the professor. “While Mamdani spoke about Umar Khalid, what prevents him from even mentioning – let alone pleading for – names like Sharjeel Imam?”

He says figures like Mamdani or left-wing liberals in India “find it convenient to speak for Umar Khalid because he is ‘secular’, in that he doesn’t posit himself as a Muslim nor uses the vocabulary of Islam to articulate his politics”.

“But these figures maintain an eerie silence about Imam, who conducts his politics in an Islamic vocabulary … The eloquence of liberals about Khalid and their silence about Imam is a sign of intellectual confusion, if not moral cowardice.”

When asked if he foresees Imam playing a role in an intellectual project of Muslim empowerment, Ahmad said while he had “no secret key to unlock the future”, he did fear that the “current regime is set to suppress such voices”.

“In some ways, the treatment of Imam by the regime resonates with the imprisonment of Italy’s Antonio Gramsci in 1926. At Gramsci’s trial, the prosecutor said: ‘For 20 years, we must stop this brain from functioning.’ Imam has already been unjustly languishing in jail for nearly seven years.”

Ahmad concluded by citing the 19th-century philosopher Henry David Thoreau to highlight the imprisonment of Imam, Khalid and other “prisoners of conscience” – both Muslims and non-Muslims.

“’The true place for a just man’ in an unjust order ‘is also a prison’,” he said.

articles.title: Devon Airbnb host felt 'violated' after house trashed during stay
articles.summary: An Airbnb host says it was "carnage" inside her house after it was damaged during a stay.
articles.body:
An Airbnb host has described being too upset to return to her own home after it was trashed during a party.

Leanne Duff, from Plymouth, Devon, said she felt "violated" after every room in her house was damaged in April, including her 13-year-old son's bedroom.

She said food was smeared over the walls, internal doors were removed and stacked in a room, a TV was smashed and her son's electric guitar had its strings cut and his toys ripped.

Airbnb said it had removed a teenager who booked the property from its platform and reimbursed Duff the cost of damage to the property, while police said they could not prove among those present who caused it.

The minimum age to create an account and book a property on Airbnb is 18 and the firm said hosts and guests must complete an identity verification process.

Airbnb said "no verification system is foolproof" but identity checks across the platform were "designed to help users have greater confidence that people on Airbnb are who they say they are".

Duff, who rents out her home when she is not there to supplement her income, has been a host for seven years and has 200 positive reviews.

She said she had never had an issue before but knew something was amiss when she returned to the property to notice her window was wide open and her sofa cushions in the street.

Recalling when she stepped inside, she said: "I can only be described it as carnage.

"Doors had been taken off their hinges and carried upstairs, food from my cupboard had been cooked and thrown at and smeared on the walls, the TV was smashed, my clothes were ripped, all the drawers had been opened and my jewellery had been thrown everywhere.

"I was stunned, shocked and heartbroken. They didn't steal anything though."

Duff called police and went to stay with her mother while an investigation was carried out.

Assessors estimated there was £25,000 worth of damage to the property, she said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said a 17-year-old girl who booked the property "was spoken to and given words of advice".

"The matter was filed due to it being impossible to prove out of those present who caused the damage or how it was caused," a spokesperson said.

Duff said she could not fault the way Airbnb handled her case but she now felt nervous about people's intentions.

She has since heightened her vetting and no longer rents her house for just one night.

She said: "I lost my livelihood for months and they wrecked a family home.

"I want to hate the people who did this but I don't because they're just people making stupid decisions and I hope they don't do it to anyone else."

A spokesperson for Airbnb said: "Disruptive parties are banned on Airbnb. We removed this guest from the platform for violating our strict policies and reimbursed the host for the damages.

"Issues on Airbnb are exceptionally rare, and our dedicated 24/7 Neighbour Support line allows anyone with concerns about a listing to contact us at any time, and we investigate all reports received."

articles.title: CERT-In issues critical alert on AI-powered cyberattacks targeting banks, fintech firms
articles.summary: India’s cyber agency CERT-In has issued a critical-severity advisory on a growing campaign of AI-assisted attacks on banks, lenders and payment firms.
articles.body: India’s cyber agency CERT-In has issued a critical-severity advisory on a growing campaign of AI-assisted attacks on banks, lenders and payment firms. It warns that the threat is active and still escalating. The advisory, CIAD-2026-0058, was issued on November 4. It updates an October 9 advisory (CIAD-2026-0046) on attackers exploiting payment and disbursement APIs to make unauthorised fund transfers. CERT-In said continued analysis of reported incidents showed a significant escalation since then.Who is being targetedThe affected entities include non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech firms, payment aggregators and payment service providers. Cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers are also on the list.CERT-In’s financial-sector response team, CSIRT-Fin, has named the attacker “CRAFTY FALCON.” It describes the actor as AI-assisted, one that surveys targets with machine intelligence, works at machine speed and strikes by calling the victim’s own payment and disbursement APIs.Repeat attacksCSIRT-Fin continues to receive reports of successful attacks. These include entities that had received earlier restricted advisories and had already carried out remediation. Some firms were deliberately attacked again after incomplete clean-ups, and attacks were timed for holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection.AI tools behind the attacksCERT-In said the attackers are using several publicly available AI offensive-security tools, including the ARTEX family of LLM-based tools, the PentAGI autonomous multi-agent penetration testing system, the Cairn attack search engine and the CyberStrikeAI framework. The agency said these tools run complete attack chains on their own, generate and refine large numbers of tailored scripts in quick succession, and adapt payloads based on how the target responds. The attackers’ infrastructure changes IP addresses within hours or days.How the attacks workThe advisory lists these patterns:* Cloud abuse: Attackers misuse cloud management and serverless services, such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda, to run commands and deploy malicious files, blending in with legitimate activity.* Weak entry points: Internet-exposed test and staging environments are used as a way in, then attackers move to production using shared credentials, tokens or network paths.* Tampered apps: Attackers reverse-engineer application code and send unauthorised API calls using modified app packages, defeating controls that assume only the genuine app will call the APIs.* Allow-list bypass: Traffic is routed through shared third-party fetcher services, such as content-acceleration and app-store review fetchers, to get around IP allow-lists.* Test transactions: Attackers send micro-value payments, such as Rs 1, to check that unauthorised fund flows work before moving large sums.* Settlement APIs: Merchant settlement APIs at payment aggregators are abused to move money.* Fast exploitation of new flaws: Newly published vulnerabilities, including file-upload and deserialisation flaws, are exploited as soon as they become public, leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications.* Crypto theft: Wallet keys are stolen from crypto exchanges and funds siphoned out.* AI-generated scripts: Large numbers of near-identical custom scripts appear in quick succession, a pattern CERT-In says is consistent with AI-generated code.What firms are told to doCERT-In asked financial entities to treat the campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. Its recommendations include:* 24x7 monitoring with extra staffing and lower alert thresholds on holidays and weekends.* Assuming attackers persist after any incident, with full forensic clean-up and regular threat hunting.* Strict separation of test and staging environments from production.* Server-side validation of every transaction, API request signing and app attestation, rather than trusting client apps.* Replacing IP allow-listing of shared fetcher pools with identity-based controls such as mutual TLS or signed requests.* Flagging micro-value test payments to new beneficiaries followed by large transfers, and holding or reviewing those flows.* Maker-checker approval and reconciliation for merchant settlement instructions.* Hardware security modules or cold storage and multi-signature approvals for crypto wallet keys.* Banning unauthorised AI offensive tools on corporate systems and watching for LLM API traffic from servers.* Rapid patching of internet-facing applications, honeypots and canary credentials as early-warning measures, and zero-trust architecture.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Filipino engineer who developed a sensor to identify potentially unsafe buildings after earthquakes has won the 2026 James Dyson global sustainability award and £30,000 for his invention, Sentinel
articles.summary: A Filipino structural engineer who developed a sensor to detect hidden damage in buildings after earthquakes has won the 2026 James Dyson Award's Global
articles.body: A Filipino structural engineer who developed a sensor to detect hidden damage in buildings after earthquakes has won the 2026 James Dyson Award's Global Sustainability prize. Aldrei Ong, a graduate of De La Salle University in the Philippines, received the recognition for his invention, Sentinel, which could help engineers identify buildings at risk of collapse. The award, announced on Wednesday, comes with £30,000 to support further development of the technology.According to the Dyson's website, Sentinel is designed to address a problem that often arises after earthquakes. Although a building may appear safe from the outside, its concrete structures can have cracks or internal damage that are difficult to detect. Such damage can make it dangerous for people to continue using the building.Determining whether these structures are safe usually requires visual inspections and specialist testing. The process becomes particularly difficult after a major earthquake, when several buildings may need to be checked at the same time. These assessments can take considerable time and money, potentially delaying decisions about whether people can safely return.Ong's invention aims to make that process easier by allowing engineers to monitor changes inside concrete structures. The sensor can detect changes associated with damage and send information to engineers, helping them identify structures that may need closer examination.How Sentinel worksThe technology is built around a concrete spacer block, a small component used during construction to keep reinforcing steel in the correct position. Ong has developed a version of this block that can also function as a damage sensor.Sentinel uses a material known as self-sensing concrete. It contains conductive materials that allow electricity to pass through it. When the concrete develops cracks or suffers damage, its electrical resistance changes. By measuring these changes, the system can provide an indication of possible structural damage.Electrodes embedded inside the block connect it to a small electronic module. The module compares the electrical resistance with the sensor's original reading. If it detects a significant change, the information is transmitted wirelessly to an online dashboard.Engineers can use this dashboard to monitor a building's condition remotely and observe changes over time.The design also aims to keep installation costs low. Since concrete spacer blocks are already used in reinforced concrete construction, Sentinel can be incorporated into new buildings without requiring an additional structural component.More than 125 concrete samples testedOng developed Sentinel through his master's research into self-sensing concrete. The work involved repeated experiments to understand how the material responds to pressure, loading and cracking.Over more than a year, he mixed, cured and tested more than 125 concrete samples. These experiments helped him refine the material and examine the relationship between structural damage and changes in electrical resistance.The invention has now moved beyond laboratory testing. Sentinel sensors have been embedded in a building in the Philippines for real-world monitoring.However, further validation is still planned. Ong intends to improve the electronic components by replacing the current hand-soldered circuitry with a custom printed circuit board. He also wants to develop versions that could be installed in existing buildings, rather than only in structures under construction.Speaking about the recognition, Ong said, "Becoming the Global Sustainability Winner of the James Dyson Award means a great deal to me, not only because of the impact Sentinel could have, but because it affirms what persistence, curiosity and a willingness to keep improving can achieve,"He added that the award had given him greater confidence to continue developing the technology and work towards making buildings safer.Dyson on invention's potentialSir James Dyson, founder of Dyson, praised Sentinel for its approach to detecting damage that may otherwise remain unnoticed. "After an earthquake, serious damage inside a concrete building can be invisible and potentially fatal," he said.Dyson said the invention could help identify problems before they become more expensive to address and reduce the risk of people occupying buildings that might collapse.Dr Bernardo Lejano, professor of structural engineering at De La Salle University's Department of Civil Engineering, also welcomed Ong's achievement. articles.title: Northampton pet budgie that hid in drain during storm rescued
articles.summary: Luna flew out of a window during Storm Boelo and found a "hidey hole" to take refuge, owner says.
articles.body:
A pet budgie who ruffled a few feathers after she escaped from her home during a storm has been rescued after taking refuge in a drain a mile (1.6km) away.

Luna's unexpected journey started when a window of the Northampton flat where she lives blew open during last month's Storm Boelo.

She was fortuitously spotted by a passing motorist who called the RSPCA after seeing Luna jump down a drain.

Richard Durant, an RSPCA inspector, found the 11-month-old in her "hidey hole" on 26 October and with colleague Rosie Cowie managed to free her.

Durant said: "Luna hadn't gone far when we believe she must have been frightened by something and she hopped down into a drain to hide.

"Luckily, in a bizarre turn of events, a passing driver happened to spot her jump down into the drain and called us for help.

"Luna saw it as a hidey hole, but if she hadn't been seen then no-one would have known she was down there."

Cowie, a trainee animal rescue officer, said: "We peered down the drain and there was Luna's little beak peeking out from a pipe.

"I gently grabbed her and popped her in a pet carrier; my first rescue, and one I certainly won't be forgetting."

Luna's owner, Cimberley Frost, said: "Luna had been watching us eat in the living room when all of a sudden we realised it had gone quiet.

"We went to look for her in the kitchen and noticed the window was open. We left it open hoping she might come back and went out to try to find her."

Frost said she played budgie noises to see if Luna would find her way home.

She then posted that Luna was missing on social media and someone got in touch to say that they had heard the RSPCA had picked her up.

Frost said: "The house was so quiet without her; she's always squeaking and talking.

"We really missed her; now she's back to being lady of the house.

"It's her first adventure, and hopefully her last."
